runs.text: Palha mais interior, & ſolida que fica

lines.note: Sube is the inner, firmer rice straw left after threshing. The initial is S, not the OCR B; mais also replaces the misread meis, and the explanation continues without a full stop.

runs.text: do arroz depois de tirado o grão.

lines.note: This completes the definition of Sube: the straw remains after the grain has been removed from the rice. The continuation belongs to the preceding noun, not to the following verb.
The verb paradigm sube, suburu, subeta is glossed as narrowing or blocking something. The following examples distinguish obstruction from more figurative drawing-in or humble behavior.
Michiuo suburu means blocking a road. The paragraph sign then opens Fito ni cuchiuo suburu, with Fito physically divided Fi-/to across this and the next line.

runs.text: to ni cuchiuo ſuburu. l, ſubete moſu.

lines.note: The example means humbly entreating someone, with subete mosu offered as an alternative expression. The damaged particle reads ni, and the alternative marker is l, rather than i,; the Portuguese Ro- continues as gar.
The Portuguese completes Rogar humilmente a alguem, to entreat someone humbly. Vouo suburu then introduces the separate example of drawing in the tail, explained in the next line.

runs.text: Meter o rabo entre as pernas com medo, &c.

lines.note: This explains Vouo suburu as putting the tail between the legs out of fear. It belongs to the preceding Japanese example and illustrates a concrete drawing-in sense.
Catauo suburu is explained as drawing in the shoulders. The following line specifies that this is a gesture of humility rather than an unqualified physical contraction.
Humilhandoſe completes the shoulder example: the person draws in the shoulders while humbling himself. It is a short continuation, not a separate headword or omitted Japanese expression.
Suberagui, equated with Teivo, denotes a king or emperor. The historical headword spelling and the printed accent in Teivǒ are retained rather than replaced by a modern Japanese form.
Suberi, suberu, subetta means to slip or slide. The headword has a damaged r, not a word division; the Portuguese historical spelling reſuelar is retained as printed.
Michiga suberu describes a slippery road. The scan has a paragraph sign before Michiga, and Eſcorregar is one word; both were mishandled by the OCR.
Curaiuo suberu means falling from a rank or dignity. The middle of Curaiuo is abraded, but the surviving letters and the Portuguese explanation favor that reading over the OCR Cuiaiuo.

Gojenga suberu refers to the tables or meal trays being taken away after eating. The initial word reads Gojenga, not Ciujenga; the printed Portuguese Aleuantarenſe is retained, with me- continuing as ſas.
The Portuguese completes the removal of tables after a meal. Cuchiga subetta then introduces a slip of the tongue; the verb has u, not the OCR o.
Subette mǒxita is given as an alternative to Cuchiga subetta. Both introduce the first-person explanation that the speaker spoke heedlessly, with deſatentadamen- continued on the next line.

runs.text: te, ou o que não deuera.

lines.note: This completes the slip-of-the-tongue explanation: the speaker spoke heedlessly or said what he should not have said. It belongs to both preceding Japanese alternatives.

runs.text: Em ſumma, ou juntamente todos, ou

lines.note: Subete is glossed as in sum, all together, or generally. The worn vowel in the headword is u, consistent with the surrounding entries, rather than the OCR a.
Cõmummente supplies the last adverbial gloss for Subete, meaning commonly or generally. The printed word is kept together rather than split into cõmum mente.
Subiqi names a slight trial pull on a bowstring; Subiqiuo suru introduces the action. The worn headword reads Subiqi rather than Sabiqi, and the Portuguese pou- continues on the next line.

runs.text: co pella corda do arco pera ver ſe eſtà teſa, ou

lines.note: This continues the bowstring example: one pulls slightly to see whether the string is taut or slack. Eſtà corrects the OCR eslà, while the old spelling pella is retained.
Froxa completes the contrast with teſa: the bowstring may be slack rather than taut. The single word is a genuine physical continuation of the preceding definition.

runs.text: Prouar a corda do arco ſe eſtà

lines.note: Subiqi, subiqu, subijta is the verb for testing a bowstring. The initial vowel is worn but agrees with the neighboring noun Subiqi; the Portuguese continues into the next line.

runs.text: teſa puxando hum pouco por ella. ¶

lines.note: The bowstring is tested by pulling it a little to see whether it is taut. Hum replaces the misread ham; Fito- then begins a new, figurative example continued below.

Fitono cocorouo subijte miru figuratively means trying or testing someone. Subijte is the preferred reading of the abraded verb, with its t especially weak; the surviving form and the preceding subijta paradigm support it.

runs.text: uar, ou experimentar a alguem. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The figurative gloss completes Prouar, ou experimentar a alguem, to test someone. Item then opens a further sense involving pain rather than continuing the psychological example.

runs.text: Doer, ou ſentir algũa dor que vai correndo

lines.note: The additional sense is aching or feeling a pain that travels along the body. This is the historical dictionary description, completed by its reference to veins and corrimentos below.

runs.text: pellas veas, ou corpo como corrimentos. Vt,

lines.note: The pain is described as running through the veins or body like corrimentos. The final Vt, introduces the Japanese example on the following line; no modern medical identification is imposed.
Sugiga subiqu is glossed as having the pain of corrimentos. The damaged Portuguese word reads corrimentos, not corsimentes; the final X. is a separate usage label.
Subitçu denotes a small hearth or brazier in which a fire is made. The location of this appliance is supplied by the short continuation on the next line.
Na caſa completes the definition of Subitçu: the small hearth or brazier is used in the house. It does not belong to the following verb entry.
Subomari, subomaru, subomatta means to close or narrow itself. The long ſ in eſtreitarſe is visible, and the alternatives remain joined by the printed l, marker.
Saxicaſaga subomaru describes a handheld parasol closing. The paragraph sign was omitted by OCR; the Portuguese Fecharſe is one word, and ſõ- continues as breiro.

runs.text: breiro que ſe leua de mão.

lines.note: This completes ſõbreiro que ſe leua de mão, a sunshade carried in the hand. Breiro corrects the OCR bretro without expanding the printed abbreviation on the preceding line.
Subome, subomuru, subometa is the corresponding transitive verb, to draw in or close something. The headword contains a damaged m, not the OCR sequence in.
Caſauo subomuru means closing the parasol. The object ending is uo, not the OCR no, and the Japanese example illustrates the transitive verb just introduced.

Cuchiuo subomete mǒſu is explained below as speaking humbly and self-effacingly. The damaged preceding label is provisionally read Perme., apparently marking the figurative use; its middle letters remain uncertain.
The Portuguese completes Falar humilde, & encolhidamente: to speak humbly and in a self-effacing or restrained manner. Encolhidamente corrects the spurious internal o in the OCR.
Subomi, subomu, subôda means to close or contract itself. The circumflex in the contracted past form is retained exactly rather than replaced with a caron.
Cataga subôda fito describes a person with drawn-in shoulders. Cata, supported by the visible t and the shoulder gloss, replaces Caraga; the Portuguese encolhi- continues below.
This completes the description of a person contracted or hunched about the shoulders. The historical hombros is retained, and the line remains part of the preceding example.
Subori, suboru, subotta is referred to the preceding contraction sense. The following Cuchiga suboru example shifts to pronunciation; the headword has o rather than the OCR u after b.
Cuchiga suboru and cotobaga suboru introduce words being pronounced with a lene accent. The physical division subo-/ru is retained, and the Portuguese pa- continues as laura.
This completes palaura com acento lene and gives Qeô and qichô as examples. The garbled palaura and Q eo are repaired, while the historical accent terminology and printed circumflexes are preserved.
Sucado is glossed as many times. It is a separate, short entry and is not a continuation of the preceding explanation of pronunciation.
Sucagiô denotes many chapters or articles. The damaged Portuguese reads capitulos, not the OCR capit laes; the sense fits the Japanese compound while its historical spelling is left unmodernized.
Sucajǒ denotes many fortresses. The worn headword is not Datajǒ, and the gloss reads Muitas fortalezas; its final caron remains distinct from the circumflex in the preceding entry.
Sucarito and succarito are adverbial alternatives describing an arrow passing over or missing its mark. The Portuguese verb is paſſar, not the OCR peſſar, and the explanation continues below.

runs.text: por alto, ou de errar o aluo cõ a ſeta &c. ¶

lines.note: The definition specifies overshooting or missing the target with an arrow. A printed paragraph sign, not the OCR final e, introduces the example whose Sucarito is divided Suca/rito without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: Errou ẽ claro cõ o arco, &c.

lines.note: Sucarito i fazzuita is explained as missing cleanly with the bow. The i belongs to the Japanese example; it is not a Portuguese alternative marker.
Sucaſucato and ſucato receive the same meaning as Sucarito. The single and repeated forms are both retained, along with the printed long ſ rather than regularized short s.
This Sucaxi paradigm means soothing or caressing children. The principal forms are printed with ſu and caita here, unlike the distinct entry two lines below.
Mininos completes the object of soothing or caressing; Couo sucasu is the Japanese example, to soothe a child. The historical Portuguese mininos and the unpunctuated Vt are retained.
The separate Sucaxi entry means opening or making something less obstructed. The unusual printed principal forms u, caite are preserved rather than regularized to the preceding entry’s ſu, caita.
Qino yedauo sucasu introduces thinning tree branches. The Portuguese Cortã- has a visible abbreviation tilde and continues as do, rather than the OCR Corti-.

runs.text: do os ramos baſtos dalgũa aruore deſabafalla.

lines.note: Cutting the dense branches opens up or airs a tree. The long ſ in baſtos and the printed nasal abbreviation in dalgũa are retained; this is one continuation of Cortãdo.
Itauo sucasu means making openings or holes in a board. The visible end is bura-, not the OCR bara, and the word continues as cos on the next line.
Buracos na taboa completes the board example. Touo aqete cajeuo sucasu then introduces opening a door to let wind through; taboa and ſucaſu correct the OCR Iaboa and ſutaſu.

runs.text: Abrir a porta de maneira que paße o ven-

lines.note: The door is opened so that the wind can pass through. The Portuguese paße uses the printed ligature, and ven- continues as to on the next line.
De parte a parte completes the explanation of wind passing through from one side to the other. This line closes the door-and-wind example rather than beginning a new sense.
Sucaxo means many places. The example Sucaxono teuo vô applies that multiplicity to wounds, with its final verb placed on the next physical line.
Vô completes the Japanese example, translated as receiving many wounds. The damaged Portuguese word is Receber, not Receler, and the Japanese period is outside the italic gloss.
Succarito is a cross-reference back to Sucarito, where both variants were already defined. The headword is not duplicated accidentally and remains a separate entry.
This Sucǒ denotes muchness, multiplication or quantity. The word quantidade crosses the physical boundary as quantida-/de; the hyphen and missing letters are restored from the scan.
Ippôno xoua sucǒno naqiuo yoſu introduces a letter causing abundant weeping. The two different long-o marks in Ippôno and sucǒno are retained rather than harmonized.

The Portuguese explains that one letter caused much weeping. Renewed close inspection supports retaining the baseline yoſu without supplying a vowel accent; the final S. remains a separate usage label.
The second Sucǒ means a poor eagle, equated with Axiqi co. The damaged form preferred after Melius is read Socucǒ, not Sorucǒ; its third letter remains a nonblocking uncertainty.

runs.text: Falcão nouo q̃ ſahio hà pouco do ninho.

lines.note: Sucobore is a young falcon that has recently left its nest. Falcão, q̃, hà and ninho repair damaged OCR without expanding the abbreviation or modernizing the grave accent.
Sucoburu is an adverb meaning much or greatly. The following example demonstrates the degree of failure to fulfill an obligation, rather than supplying a separate headword.
Sucoburu fonyuo somuqu is explained as greatly failing in one’s duty. The damaged verb is ſomuqu, not the OCR ſumauqu; the Portuguese explanation continues below.

runs.text: cõ ſeu deuer como cõ obrigação de viſitar, &c.

lines.note: This completes the duty example, specifying obligations such as paying a visit. Deuer corrects druer, while the printed cõ abbreviations remain unexpanded.
Sucocu, paraphrased as Cazuno toqi, denotes many hours. The Japanese paraphrase is not an embedded Portuguese term and is therefore not marked for optional typeface toggling.
Sucoxi means a little. The Portuguese Humpouco is printed tightly together and is retained as in the baseline rather than silently modernized to two words.
Sucui, sucǔ, sucǔta means taking something with a spoon or cupped hand. Both length marks are carons; the third form is ǔta, not a partly italic àta.

runs.text: lher. l, com a mão à maneira de colher: Vt,

lines.note: The definition allows either a spoon or a hand held like one. The end reads colher: Vt, rather than colhes Vt.; the following line supplies the utensil example.

Saixi and jacuxi occur in the example of scooping rice. The damaged Saixi is retained provisionally, including uncertainty about the faint mark immediately after it; jacuxi, mexiuo and ſucǔ correct the clearer OCR errors.
The first example means taking rice with a spoon. Vuouo sucǔ then introduces catching fish with a particular net, described in the next line; cõ retains its abbreviation.
The fishing net is compared to a còuão. Item introduces a separate Sucui, ǔ sense, to deliver or save; the damaged u in còuão and the caron in ǔ are restored.

The new sense is saving or delivering. Banmino vreiuo sucǔ is the preferred reading of the heavily abraded example, meaning relieving the people’s distress; Banmino in particular remains uncertain in its medial letters.

runs.text: Liurar o pouo de moleſtias, & triſtezas.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains delivering the people from afflictions and sorrows. This confirms the sense of the preceding damaged Japanese example without requiring a modernized Japanese spelling.

runs.text: Certa rede como cõuão que tem hum

lines.note: Sucui ami names a particular net compared to a cõuão. The printed separation of the Japanese elements and the Portuguese nasal marks are retained, despite lexical indexes joining the headword.
The net has a long handle for taking fish. Comprido and tomar replace the OCR cemprido and tomur; the line completes the preceding implement definition.
Sucui tori, sucui toru, sucui totta means catching or taking fish with that net. The past ending reads otta, not outa, and the Portuguese pei- continues below.

runs.text: xe com eſta rede, ou còuão. Itẽ, Permet. Li-

lines.note: This completes catching fish with the net or còuão. The entry then marks a metaphorical sense with Itẽ, Permet., introducing deliverance or rescue on the next line.
Liurar, ou ſaluar supplies the figurative meaning of Sucui tori: to deliver or save. The physical Li-/urar division is retained rather than joined in the canonical text.

Sucume, sucumuru, sucumeta means constraining or repressing. Renewed close inspection supports the anomalous printed Conſrenger; no t is supplied and the spelling is not normalized to constranger. Repri- continues as mir.
Fitouo sucumuru illustrates constraining someone. A paragraph sign then starts Fito-/uo tori sucumuru, a more explicit example of physically holding a person.
Fitouo tori sucumuru means forcibly keeping hold of someone. The source has por- at the physical end, even though the next line begins the separate word força; that printed hyphen is retained.

runs.text: força de maneira que não bula.

lines.note: This completes holding someone by force so that the person cannot move. Maneira replaces the OCR manena, while the historical verb form bula is retained.
Sucumete is an adverb meaning by force or by constraining. Por força corrects Per ferça, and the abbreviation in conſtrangẽdo is preserved.
Sucumi, sucumu, sucũda describes being immobilized or stiff. The tilde over the past-form u is visible; the worn Portuguese adjective is provisionally read tolheito, followed by eſtar to-/do hirto.
The Portuguese completes being entirely stiff. Tachimachi gotaimo su-/cunde begins an example of the limbs suddenly contracting; gotaimo repairs the OCR’s artificial punctuation and gap.
This completes sucunde and explains the limbs immediately drawing in or becoming immobile. The sentence continues below, so the final ou is retained without supplied punctuation.

The Portuguese finishes the immobility explanation. Vmano axiga begins the next example about a horse’s legs; the lower-right ſucunda. is classified as a catchword by placement, without a supplied next page to verify repetition.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: The lower-right ſucunda. is treated as a catchword on positional evidence. The next page was not supplied, so its anticipated repetition has not been independently checked.

lines.note: The lower-right placement below the last body row favors a catchword. Its text anticipates the completion of Vmano axiga; repetition on the unsupplied following page has not been verified.
